items.article_search_text: The Baku City Circuit’s combination of long straights, heavy braking zones and narrow Old City corners demands precision, commitment and carefully balanced car set-ups, drivers say. The Baku City Circuit’s combination of long straights, heavy braking zones and narrow Old City corners demands precision, commitment and carefully balanced car... Baku’s combination of high-speed straights and tight corners makes it one of Formula 1’s most unusual and demanding venues, Mercedes driver George Russell told Anadolu Agency.McLaren’s Oscar Piastri said the Azerbaijan capital’s street circuit requires “pure commitment”, while circuit designer Carsten Tilke said its character is closely tied to Baku’s historic setting and existing streets.Ahead of Saturday’s 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix, the drivers and designer described the features that have made the Baku City Circuit one of the sport’s most distinctive venues.The 6.003-kilometre street circuit, which hosted Formula 1 for the first time in 2016, takes cars from one of the calendar’s longest straights into heavy braking zones and the narrow streets surrounding Baku’s Old City. A small error can send a car into the barriers and end a driver’s race.Two contrasting challenges in one lapRussell, who secured pole position in Friday’s qualifying session, said Baku presents “two very different challenges” during a single lap.“You’ve got one of the longest straights of the season where you’re reaching incredibly high speeds, and then you've got the tight, technical sections through the Old City where there's absolutely no margin for error,” he told Anadolu Agency.Russell said the circuit is neither a conventional street track nor a traditional racing venue. Its long straights, heavy braking areas and extremely narrow corners make it “one of the most unusual and demanding events of the year”.The section around the Old City walls is the part drivers most readily associate with Baku, he said, because its tight corners leave almost no room for mistakes.“You need to balance commitment with discipline. In Baku, the walls are always there waiting for you, but if you focus on that too much, you end up driving below the limit,” Russell said. He added that drivers must prepare thoroughly, build confidence in practice and trust their instincts during the race.He also pointed to the contrast between Baku’s modern skyline and historic centre as another feature that sets the circuit apart.Overtaking and set-up compromisesPiastri said Baku differs from many other street circuits because its long straights provide genuine opportunities to overtake.“This presents good opportunities to recover that don’t exist elsewhere,” he told Anadolu Agency. However, low tyre degradation limits the strategic alternatives available to teams, meaning overtaking is often the main way for a driver to regain positions.Although the track changes sharply from ultra-fast sections to the narrow Old City, Piastri said drivers do not necessarily need to adopt a different mindset during each lap. Maintaining concentration, however, becomes even more important.The contrasting high- and low-speed sections also create a difficult engineering compromise between downforce, drag and mechanical grip. Cars built around higher-downforce packages can be competitive at tracks such as Silverstone and Barcelona but may struggle in Baku, where teams generally favour lower downforce to improve straight-line speed.“Like every street circuit, Baku is one that requires pure commitment,” Piastri said, describing the combination of fast sectors and technical corners as a challenge for drivers and engineers, as well as an entertaining spectacle for fans.A circuit shaped by BakuTilke, one of the designers involved in creating the circuit, said the original goal was to make the track inseparable from the city around it.“As a street circuit, the existing road network and city infrastructure naturally defined many of the possibilities and constraints for the layout,” he told Anadolu Agency. The designers identified the streets that could provide the best racing experience and connected them to form a challenging circuit.Baku’s Old City was intended to play a central role from the outset, Tilke said. Its inclusion gave the circuit a distinctive identity and established a strong connection with the capital.He said the contrast between the track’s very fast and extremely narrow sections emerged largely from the existing road network. The challenge was to connect those roads into a coherent racing circuit.A decade after Baku joined the Formula 1 calendar, Tilke said the venue had developed a strong and distinctive identity. While some details could potentially be refined, he argued that any changes should preserve the features that make the circuit recognisable.“Its identity is closely connected to the city, its historic setting and the existing streets,” Tilke said. “Any potential changes should therefore support the circuit’s development without changing what makes it distinctive.” Latest news from Azerbaijan and the world - politics, economy, sports, culture and society

Oscar Piastri acknowledged McLaren had no chance of outpacing George Russell to pole position during qualifying at the Formula 1 Azerbaijan GP, despite finding some ‘surprise’ pace. Piastri will start in third behind Russell and Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc for Saturday’s race in Baku, with teammate and reigning world champion Lando Norris claiming fifth. It’s the sixth time this season the Australian driver has out-qualified Norris for a Grand Prix. Oscar Piastri and Charles Leclerc had no answer for George Russell Piastri welcomes ‘surprise’ McLaren pace The result comes after a tricky start to the weekend for McLaren, who found themselves some way down the leaderboard during the earlier free practice sessions. The team found additional pace during Friday’s qualifying session, but were no match for Russell, whose dominant lap cleared Piastri by more than eight tenths. Piastri, however, was pleased by the result, with the team having brought a significant body package upgrade ahead of the weekend in an attempt to boost its straightline speed. “We found a bit of pace. It's not the first time that's happened to us this year,” he said. “We seem like we're a bit on the back foot through practice. “We've come out in qualifying, and we just find that bit extra. I was pretty surprised to see us one-two after the first lap of Q3, but unfortunately, we had no hope against George. “I'm happy with how the weekend's gone so far. It's never easy around here, especially when it's so gusty like today, so I'm very happy to be back in the top three.” Strong winds in Baku can make it difficult to predict the cars’ balances, particularly in exposed parts of the track. Asked how he manages these challenges, Piastri responded: “Honestly, trying to keep it between the lines, the highway lines down the straights, not easy, especially it always sounds so dull talking about the wind in a Formula 1 car, but even when the walls disappear and you get a bit more open, you really get a massive gust, so it's not easy at all. “There's 30- or 40kph difference sometimes between laps, so you’ve really got to be on your toes and adapt on the fly.” READ MORE -

items.article_search_text: McLaren CEO Zak Brown sparked backlash for his "wide open" comments for Max Verstappen to join the team. F1 fans accused him of throwing Oscar Piastri under the bus, fueling speculation that Piastri could eventually lose his seat to Verstappen, despite Lando Norris being secure.﻿ "The door is still wide open for Max. For 2028, 2029, or any year for that matter. Just before the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, which takes place in Baku on Saturday, McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown sparked another controversy after admitting that he has kept the door “wide open” for Red Bull driver Max Verstappen to join the team in the future.Now, his recent remarks come right after the Dutch racer committed to his immediate future with Red Bull. Although Brown did not confirm that McLaren is preparing to replace either of its current drivers, these comments sparked speculation about who is going to be the driver Verstappen will replace. Some fans have deduced that it is none other than Oscar Piastri who is getting “thrown” under the bus. As Lando Norris won the Drivers’ Championship in 2025, and McLaren secured the Constructors’ title, it seems it is Oscar who might get replaced, even though Brown described him previously as a future World Champion.Zak Brown recently acknowledged Max Verstappen as one of Formula 1’s biggest stars. On September 25, while speaking to Dutch newspaper De Telegraaf, he explained that he had several conversations with Verstappen during the summer and also made a few comments.It follows, “The door is still wide open for Max. For 2028, 2029 or any year, for that matter. I enjoyed getting to know him better and would love to work with him someday…I was much more impressed by him as an individual than I had expected. I feel like I can really race with this guy, because I hate racing against him.”This is significant because Verstappen, 28, has now signed a long-term deal with Red Bull, and Lando Norris is considered the “golden anchor” and extremely protected. That leaves Oscar Piastri in a dangerous situation. Even though Brown did not comment on whom he will replace, that did not stop the fans from starting a whole new online speculation.Lando Norris has become the McLaren Formula 1 Team’s long-term cornerstone after winning his first Drivers’ Championship in 2025. Piastri established himself as a genuine Championship contender and finished third. Both of them won seven races during the last campaign.So until F1 suddenly gives McLaren a third car, somebody is definitely going under the bus. A fan remarked, “The way Zak is openly offering to throw Oscar under the bus. What a vile person.” Another wrote, “This is the part where I know Zak is going to stab Oscar in the back?”Max Verstappen fans reacted differently, saying, “McLaren is lucky Oscar is a chill guy. Max would smack tf out of Zak Brown if he ever tried that papaya rule bs on him.” One commented, “Leave Max alone.”With Piastri’s contract ending in 2028, fans genuinely questioned, "So is Piastri gone after 2027?”Even though Max is under contract till 2030 and admitted that he is loyal to Red Bull, Brown’s comments triggered bitterness internally in McLaren.For now, none of this has been confirmed, and the rest remains online speculation. What is clear, however, is that Brown has deliberately kept the door open for Verstappen. The Norris-Piastri partnership was expected to be the foundation of McLaren’s new era, but Brown’s latest comments have certainly raised questions about what the team’s future could look like.The 51-lap 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix will take place on Saturday, September 26, 2026. This adjustment has been made due to the Annual Remembrance Day of Azerbaijan on September 27. It will happen at the Baku City Circuit and start at 15:00 local time (AZT). As for Brown’s comments, neither driver has publicly responded to the statement so far.

items.article_search_text: Kimi Antonelli insists the Formula 1 title race is “not over” as he takes a vast 81-point lead into this week's Azerbaijan Grand Prix. It looks as good as… Kimi Antonelli insists the Formula 1 title race is “not over” as he takes a vast 81-point lead into this week's Azerbaijan Grand Prix. It looks as good as over, but Baku has sprung surprises before. A year ago, that was where Oscar Piastri's title shot began to fall apart. The Australian was leading the standings when he almost stalled on the grid, dropped to last and crashed, all in the space of about a minute on the opening lap.That kicked off a run of six races without a podium finish for Piastri, who had to watch the title race become a fight between eventual champion Lando Norris and Max Verstappen.Antonelli — whose practice was hampered by car problems Thursday — is sounding cautious as he aims to become F1's youngest-ever champion. “Until you cross that finish line, it’s not over. It’s like tennis, one point at a time, here one race at a time," he said. “The sooner it’s over, the better it is. Still a long way and it’s not going to be easy. It’s going to be intense but I’m ready to give my best and to keep having fun.”There are key differences this year. For one thing, Antonelli’s lead is more than double the biggest advantage Piastri had last year. He’s coming off back-to-back wins, not the team orders controversy which was dogging Piastri and Norris a year ago. As for Piastri, he says it's “love-hate in some ways” as he returns to a venue where he won in 2024 and endured a nightmare 2025. “I think probably my best race ever has been at this track and probably my worst race ever has been at this track, so always eventful,” Piastri said.Russell fastest in practice as Antonelli has car troubleAntonelli’s teammate George Russell was dominant in Friday's first practice, going fastest by four-tenths of a second after Antonelli's session was interrupted a hydraulic failure which left his car smoking at the side of the track. Verstappen was second-fastest for Red Bull, with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc third and Lewis Hamilton fourth amid a spate of technical issues for various cars. Antonelli was fifth-fastest. McLaren struggled with Piastri sixth and Lando Norris 14th.Antonelli's title rivals need to bounce backThe three British drivers behind Antonelli are all trying to recover from disappointing races at the Spanish Grand Prix two weeks ago.Russell all but ruled himself out of the title race after an uncompetitive run to fifth in Madrid, while Norris was left ruing a badly-timed virtual safety car which cost him the win. Hamilton retired, making it five races off the podium for the Ferrari driver.“I’m going to keep fighting every single race until it’s mathematically impossible, but it doesn’t change how I go about my job," Russell said Wednesday. "There’s obviously a huge deficit, but it’s not even really a consideration right now.”Red Bull's double bet on Isack HadjarRed Bull is backing Isack Hadjar's health and his potential in the hope the young French driver develops into one of F1's top talents.Hadjar returns for Baku despite saying he still feels pain from the wrist fracture which ruled him out of the last three races. And he has a contract extension to partner Max Verstappen for 2027, too.Wrist injuries can have long-term consequences. Lance Stroll rushed back from wrist fractures sustained in a preseason cycling crash in 2023 but ended up missing a race after all in 2025 when he needed a follow-up operation to deal with lingering pain.A rare Saturday race amid broader F1 schedule uncertaintyIt's an unusual race week in a very unusual F1 season, as the Azerbaijan Grand Prix is held on a Saturday to make way for a national day of remembrance on Sunday. That means Thursday practice and Friday qualifying.This starts a run of three races in three weeks because of the extra round next week in Malaysia, still carrying branding of the called-off Bahrain Grand Prix. ___See AP’s full auto racing coverage here

Oscar Piastri has made a damning admission about driving the 2026 Formula 1 cars, stating that the AI reduces his input at points when out on track. Piastri is enduring a challenging season, struggling to get to grips with the new generation of car, yet to win a race in 2026. The Australian has been one of the more quieter drivers in giving his verdict on the cars, which feature a near 50:50 split in electrical and internal combustion power. But he has made an damning admission over the computer systems onboard the cars, which actively learns the circuit and how to deploy the battery during a lap. "Sometimes, yes," Piastri said to media, including Motorsport Week, if he "felt like a passenger of the AI systems". "At a track like Spa or a track like Silverstone, it’s going to be worse. At the Hungaroring or Zandvoort, I really don’t expect there to be many problems at all with that kind of thing, because the straights are so much shorter, so even if there are differences, they should be a lot less. "But the principle of driving a race car that loses effectively half of its power before the end of the straight is hard to get your head around sometimes. Oscar Piastri has made a damning admission over the AI in the current generation of F1 cars Oscar Piastri details AI issues Elaborating on his point, Piastri detailed the radical way the car learns the sectors of the legendary Spa circuit. "Even in Spa, a lot of the middle sector we were doing it just on the combustion engine, with no battery assistance at all, which is a weird feeling in itself, having some corners with a certain amount of power and others with full power. "I think Spa was particularly frustrating, not just for me but for quite a lot of others, because those small differences in the code and what the engines did made quite a big difference in lap time. "Especially at the front of the field, I think there were still only nine hundredths or something separating four positions, and there were definitely more than nine hundredths on the table for quite a few drivers from things they could not control." Piastri's feedback on the car's AI systems highlights the journey F1 faces with these regulations. For a driver to feel like a passenger is not a sentiment many will want to experience. Oscar Piastri playing cricket wasn’t on anyone’s bingo card. In a surprising crossover that has fans talking, the McLaren Formula 1 driver recently traded the racetrack for the crease.The Australian star took on a high-speed cricket challenge on his YouTube series, The Switch, hosted by former England batsman Kevin Pietersen. Filmed around mid-August 2026, the off-track session used a bowling machine to push deliveries up toward the 100mph mark just for fun.Now, F1 fans are left wondering if he can actually play the game and how he managed to handle those intense deliveries. Let's see exactly what went down!Piastri is still fully committed to McLaren and his Formula 1 career. The cricket session was just a fun, light-hearted guest appearance on Kevin Pietersen’s YouTube series, , reportedly per .Reports confirm that it was strictly a one-off challenge with a bowling machine, rather than any sort of career change or exit from the F1 grid. The McLaren driver is still racing in the 2026 season with his usual car number, 81.The Melbourne-born driver actually grew up playing junior cricket, mostly as a bowler, along with Australian Rules football before he shifted his focus entirely to karting and racing.He’s often spoken about his genuine love for the game, reportedly even heading out to watch matches like the Melbourne Test, and is good friends with players like Mitchell Starc. During the challenge, he took on deliveries from a bowling machine that started at 51 mph, playing with three “lives” as the speed progressively cranked up.Piastri managed to handle deliveries all the way up to 81 mph. Starting at 51 mph and using his three allotted lives, he steadily worked his way through the different speeds on the bowling machine, reportedly reaching 81 mph at his final attempt.That final 81 mph figure happened to perfectly match his Formula 1 race number, adding a fun coincidence to the session. Even though he didn't quite hit the maximum 100 mph target, it was still a really impressive performance for someone who isn't a professional cricketer.Clocking in at 81 mph actually puts Piastri second on challenge leaderboard. The ranking reportedly has Bollywood actor Suniel Shetty holding onto the top spot with a higher speed of around 91 to 92 mph, while tennis star Andy Murray finished just behind at 79 mph.This places the F1 driver ahead of quite a few other high-profile guests who have taken on the exact same progressive speed bowling machine test.One user on Reddit wrote, “First we had Max vs 100 drivers. Now it's Oscar vs 100 mph ball. Wonder what's next for the vs 100 series.”Another mentioned, “His first instinct is to go defensive. That's how you know he's an Aussie batter.” A third joked, “I laughed so hard when he left the ball.” Another added, “Australian player defaults to Test match mode, as per usual.”For Piastri, the cricket challenge was another reminder that his sporting talent stretches far beyond the Formula 1 circuit.
